blueprint_topic: Management of Care — durable medical equipment order, supplier coordination, coverage verification, and safe discharge resource planning
stem: A Medicare beneficiary needs a walker for safe mobility at home after hip surgery. Which nursing action best supports appropriate durable medical equipment coordination?

options.A: Coordinate the prescribed walker for home use with the discharge team and a Medicare-enrolled DME supplier, and verify assignment and expected cost-sharing.
options.B: Recommend buying a walker from a retail store first and submit the receipt later, using the provider's mobility note as the coverage documentation.
options.C: Complete the remaining discharge teaching and have the client contact a DME supplier after arriving home to begin the walker-order process.
options.D: Tell the client the prescribed walker should have no out-of-pocket cost because medical necessity determines both coverage and the final payment amount.

rationale: A is correct. Current Medicare guidance states that Part B covers medically necessary walkers when a provider prescribes the equipment for use in the beneficiary's home, and that doctors and DME suppliers should be enrolled in Medicare. Medicare also advises checking whether the supplier participates in Medicare or accepts assignment because assignment affects the beneficiary's cost. Current CMS DMEPOS guidance requires a standardized written order with beneficiary/item/practitioner/date/signature elements and requires the treating practitioner to submit the complete order to the supplier before the claim is submitted. The nurse should therefore coordinate the prescribed walker through the discharge process and an appropriate enrolled supplier while helping verify assignment and expected cost-sharing rather than guaranteeing payment. B is incorrect because a retail purchase and mobility note do not replace the Medicare supplier and standardized-order requirements. C is incorrect because a walker already identified as necessary for safe home mobility should be coordinated as part of discharge planning rather than deferred until after arrival home. D is incorrect because medical necessity does not guarantee zero out-of-pocket cost; Medicare.gov states that deductible, coinsurance, assignment, and supplier participation can affect cost.
educational_objective: Coordinate medically necessary DME for discharge by ensuring an appropriate provider order for home use, working with a Medicare-enrolled supplier, and verifying assignment/cost details rather than assuming or guaranteeing coverage.
source_organization: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS); Medicare.gov; National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)

source_locator: Medicare.gov 'Walkers' lines 10-16 and 32-46: Part B covers eligible walkers; medically necessary DME is covered when prescribed by a provider for home use; doctors and DME suppliers should be enrolled in Medicare; supplier participation/assignment should be checked; after the Part B deductible the beneficiary generally pays 20% of the Medicare-approved amount when the supplier accepts assignment, and costs may be higher if the supplier does not participate/accept assignment. Medicare.gov 'Durable medical equipment (DME) coverage' lines 23-31, 34-50, and 61-73: DME definition, walkers as covered DME, home-use provider-order requirement, Medicare enrollment and assignment/cost rules. CMS DMEPOS order-requirements lines 741-751: standardized written-order elements include beneficiary identifier, item description, quantity if applicable, treating practitioner/NPI, date and practitioner signature; the complete written order must be submitted to the supplier before claim submission. CMS lines 758-770: written-order-before-delivery and face-to-face requirements apply only to DMEPOS items selected for the Required List; other DMEPOS items require the order before claim submission. CMS lines 780-782: page last modified 07/31/2026. NCSBN 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan Management of Care printed page 7 / PDF pageno 10: discharge clients safely, verify/implement provider orders, assess referral needs, collaborate with multidisciplinary team members, update plans of care, and utilize resources.
source_claim_supported: Current Medicare/CMS sources directly support the home-use provider-order requirement, enrolled DME supplier, standardized written-order elements, assignment/cost implications, and the need not to guarantee full coverage. The item does not overstate WOPD timing requirements. NCSBN supports nursing coordination of provider orders, referrals, discharge resources, and continuity of care.

correction_summary: Original Q1874 had a 215-character correct answer, substantially shorter distractors, and an absolute-word distractor. All four options were rebuilt as realistic DME coordination decisions with similar length. The correct answer now tests provider-ordered home-use DME, Medicare-enrolled supplier coordination, assignment/cost verification, and safe discharge planning without implying that the nurse independently determines coverage or promises payment. Independent second pass additionally verified that the item does not incorrectly generalize written-order-before-delivery requirements to all DMEPOS items.

option_audit.A: Correct; integrates provider-ordered home-use walker, enrolled supplier coordination, assignment/cost verification, and discharge planning without overclaiming coverage.
option_audit.B: Plausible reimbursement shortcut; incorrect because a retail purchase plus mobility note does not substitute for the required DME order/supplier process.
option_audit.C: Plausible timing error; incorrect because the walker is already identified as necessary for safe home mobility and should be coordinated during discharge planning rather than deferred.
option_audit.D: Plausible coverage misconception; incorrect because medical necessity does not determine zero cost and Medicare cost-sharing depends on deductible, assignment and supplier participation.

cueing_audit.absolute_words: No option uses all/only/always/never/must-type absolute wording.
cueing_audit.answer_length: Final option lengths: A 156, B 147, C 139, D 152 characters; the correct answer is not uniquely long and choices are substantially balanced.
cueing_audit.grammatical_lexical: All four alternatives are action-oriented DME/discharge decisions and use credible Medicare-process language.
cueing_audit.second_answer_risk: Independent adversarial reread found no defensible second answer. B bypasses the proper order/supplier process, C defers a known discharge safety resource, and D overstates cost coverage; A is the unique best coordination response.

independent_second_pass: PASS — post-fetch adversarial reread independently rechecked stem, all A/B/C/D alternatives, correct key, rationale, objective, Medicare walker/DME coverage rules, CMS standardized-order rules, WOPD scope, supplier enrollment/assignment, cost-sharing, NCSBN Management of Care fit, cueing, role scope and second-answer risk. The nurse coordinates rather than independently prescribing or guaranteeing Medicare payment. No unresolved conflict identified.
